title: Dhanvantari rises with the nectar
hookLine: the gods and demons churn the ocean, and a healer rises holding the pot of nectar
carry: the body is the first tool of dharma
tomorrow: a woman stands in a king's hall, and the king says he doesn't remember her.
last: THE VEDAS STILL GREET EVERY DAWN.

cards: The ocean of milk is being churned. The gods pull one end of a great serpent wound around a mountain, the demons pull the other, and the sea foams and foams. Poison comes up first, and Shiva drinks it.
And then, out of the white water, a figure rises, dark and shining, holding a pot. It's Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, and the pot holds amrita, the nectar.
Today's summit sit climbs back to Ayurveda, and the god many Hindus pray to for health.

teach.b: In the Bhagavata Purana, Dhanvantari is a part of Vishnu himself, and the one who brings Ayurveda, the science of long life.

Many families honor him on Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, with a lamp and a prayer for health. Here's the teaching Hindus take from him: caring for the body isn't vanity, and it isn't separate from religion.

The poet Kalidasa put it in a line people still quote: the body is the first tool of dharma. The Charaka Samhita says it plainly: health is the root of the four aims of a life, dharma, a good living, love, and freedom.
This year we read Ayurveda's doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, like weather: a way of noticing, not a diagnosis; nothing here replaces a doctor.

The classical daily round cleans the teeth and the tongue, keeps exercise to about half your strength, and Charaka's good conduct says to greet people first. Patanjali asks for breath long and subtle, not forced.
And the Sushruta Samhita's definition of the healthy person lists a body in balance, then doesn't stop: it ends with a self, senses and mind that are clear and content.
The word for healthy, svastha, can be read as standing in yourself. So when a Hindu grandmother says eat, sleep, go for a walk, she isn't only fussing.
In this tradition, the body is where prayer, work and love happen, and tending it is part of the climb.

how: Many Hindu families honor Dhanvantari on Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, with lamps and prayers for health; some also draw on Ayurvedic ideas, such as a morning routine or seasonal eating, alongside modern medicine.

s: in Hindu teaching, caring for the body is vanity that distracts from God
Kalidasa calls the body the first tool of dharma, and Charaka calls health the root of life's aims.
Dhanvantari rose from the churning of the ocean holding the pot of amrita
the Bhagavata tells it, and calls him a part of Vishnu.
on this path, the doshas are offered as a medical diagnosis
here they're read as a way of noticing, like weather; nothing in them replaces a doctor.

games.q: exam week. you plan to skip sleep and meals to study. nani says tending your body is part of dharma. in this tradition, is she right?
o: no. religion is about the soul; the body doesn't matter.
yes. the body is the first tool of dharma, and health is the root of life's aims.
only when you're sick; healthy people can ignore the body.
games.why: Kalidasa's line and Charaka's both say it: the body is how dharma gets done, so tending it is part of the practice, not a break from it.

practice: Notice the breath as it is, without changing anything, then let the out-breath grow a little longer and quieter, long and subtle, not big and loud, letting it go back to normal if it strains.
At the end, ask the old question gently: are the senses at ease, is the mind content, even a little? Don't fix anything; just notice.
If you pray, offer a short prayer for the health of someone you love, as families do on Dhanteras.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Dhanvantari, the body as dharma's first tool, and a definition of health that ends with a mind at ease. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: svastha, healthy; it can be read as standing in oneself, the word for the well person in Sushruta's definition.
